newsitem.title: USA: Governor puts permit halt on Cook Inlet tracts.
newsitem.headline: Governor puts permit halt on Cook Inlet tracts.

text.p: Alaska Gov. Tony Knowles said Tuesday he will delay any permits for oil and gas drilling in lower Cook Inlet for three months while area residents and industry representatives attempt to compromise on how the area should be developed.

The tracts -- in the southern part of the inlet and along the Kenai River, a world-famous salmon fishing site -- are among the approximately 1 million onshore and offshore acres being offered by the state for lease on Wednesday.

"What we're doing is placing a moratorium on all permits until that time when all of the parties can get together and work it out," Knowles said at a late afternoon news conference, on the eve of the controversial lease sale.

Environmentalists, fishermen and residents of the nearby communities on Alaska's Kenai Peninsula have bitterly opposed the lease sale. They have staged demonstrations, flooded the governor's office with protest messages and filed legal challenges to the sale.
A last-minute attempt by sale opponents to have a state Superior Court judge issue a delay was denied late Tuesday.
Knowles rejected pleas that he delay, cancel or trim the sale. But he acknowledged that many area residents believe the public review process ignored their concerns.
"It's clear that the legal requirements (for the lease sale) have been met, but going by the book isn't good enough sometimes. And I certainly feel that that's the case here," he said.
The Nature Conservancy of Alaska will coordinate the meetings between area residents and the industry, Knowles said.
Cook Inlet is the site of Alaska's oldest operating oil and gas fields.

The northern part of the inlet has been developed extensively. But residents of the southern part of the inlet -- a center for commercial and sport fishing, recreation and tourism -- have long resisted efforts to drill for oil and gas there.
Knowles defended efforts to increase oil development in the area.

"We've had 40 years of oil industry on the Kenai Peninula. It built a lot of economic progress for that community," he said. "At the same time people treasure the resources and the lifestyle of those communities. I think that we can work it out together."
Affected by the moratorium would be about 40 tracts in the southern part of the inlet and fewer than 20 tracts along the Kenai River, said John Shively, state natural resources commissioner.
It is unknown whether all or any of those tracts will receive bids, Shively said.
